title: Haad wella hayy — pointing at things
goal: Point at things around you, tell a noun's gender from its ending, and use the article اَل correctly.
bekal: point at things with هَاد and هَيّ, according to the word's gender
guess a noun's gender from its last letter
tell "a thing" from "the thing" with اَل

dialogs.title: حَكِي — بِمَكْتَبِة الْجَامْعَة
dialogs.intro: The campus bookshop. Budi is looking for a textbook and asks the shopkeeper.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Hi. I'd like to ask something.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.id: Go ahead. What would you like?

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.id: This is a grammar book. A very good one.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.id: This is a magazine. It comes out every week.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.text: لَا وَاللَّه. بَسّ فِي عَرَبِي عَرَبِي.
lines.id: No, there isn't. But there's Arabic–Arabic.
lines.literal: no by-God. but there-is Arabic Arabic.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: ṭayyib. baddi el-ktaab w haad el-’aamuus.
lines.id: All right. I'd like that book and this dictionary.
lines.literal: fine. want-my the-book and this the-dictionary.

notes: **Demonstratives follow the gender of the thing, not its distance.** Use هَاد *haad* for masculine things, هَيّ *hayy* for feminine ones, هَدُول *hadōl* for any plural. And "gender" here has nothing to do with living things: كْتَاب (book) is masculine, مَجَلِّة (magazine) is feminine.

**Guessing is easy: look at the ending.** Words ending in ة are almost always feminine (مَجَلِّة · طَاوْلِة · مَدْرَسِة · شَنْطَة). Words not ending in ة are almost always masculine (كْتَاب · قَامُوس · بَاب · قَلَم). This simple rule covers about nine words out of ten.

**Levantine Arabic doesn't split "this" and "that" as sharply as English.** The form هَاد is used for both, and if needed you add هْنِيك *hniik* ("over there") or point. The form هَدَاك *hadaak* does exist for "that one", but it's much rarer.

**The word فِي means "there is", and here it's not a preposition.** The sentence فِي قَامُوس means "there's a dictionary"; مَا فِي قَامُوس means "there's no dictionary". The same word also happens to mean "in", and its place in the sentence tells them apart.

**Shopping small talk has its own formulas.** The phrase تَكْرَم عَيْنَك *takram ‘ēnak* is roughly "my pleasure", and مَبْرُوك *mabruuk* is said for any purchase, however small, and is answered with اَللَّه يْبَارِك فِيك. Learn the pairs as wholes.

**The word طَيِّب is used exactly like "OK" or "all right".** It closes one part of a conversation and opens the next. Together with يَلَّا and خَلَص, these three are the backbone of everyday conversation.

grammars.title: Demonstratives and the gender of things
after: When a demonstrative goes with a **specific** thing, the noun must take اَل — for example هَاد الْكْتَاب *haad el-ktaab* ("this book"). Without اَل the meaning becomes a full sentence: هَاد كْتَاب ("this is a book").

That difference matters and is often missed. The phrase هَيّ الْمَجَلِّة means "this magazine" — unfinished, still waiting for more. The sentence هَيّ مَجَلِّة is already complete: "this is a magazine".

grammars.title: The article اَل and the letters that swallow it
body: English marks "the" with a separate word; Arabic marks "a thing we both know about" on the word itself, and marking it is not optional.
after: The *l* of اَل melts into the next letter when that letter is one of the **sun letters** — among them ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن. You can spot it by the shadda that appears on that letter.

Worth noting for the dialect: in the Levant, اَل is almost always pronounced **el-**, not **al-** as in Fusha. The word اَلْبَيْت sounds like *el-bēt*, not *al-bait*. Two changes at once, and both mark the dialect.

blocks.text: One oddity placed in the table on purpose: كِرْسِي *kirsi* (chair) ends in ي, not ة, yet in many parts of the Levant it's still treated as **feminine**. There are a few words like this, not many — just learn them as you meet them, don't hunt for a rule.

blocks.title: Four words you may already know
items: The words كِرْسِي · قَلَم · كْتَاب and سَاعَة have traveled into many languages — Persian, Turkish, Swahili, Malay and Urdu among them — as words for chair, pen, book and hour. If you know any of those languages, these four come free.
The words تِلِفُون and كُمْبْيُوتَر come from the opposite direction — Arabic borrowed them from European languages, just as English did. You can guess hundreds of tech words this way.

blocks.text: Notice that the questions شُو هَاد and مِين هَاد use the same demonstrative; only the question word differs: شُو for things, مِين for people. Arabic never uses شُو for humans, and doing so sounds rude.

blocks.title: The word كْتِير works in two directions
items: After an adjective, كْتِير *ktiir* means "very": مْنِيح كْتِير ("very good").
Before a noun, it means "many, a lot of": كْتِير كْتُب ("lots of books").
On its own as an answer, it means "a lot" or "very" — a perfectly natural reply to the question قَدِّيش.
There's no key on the table.
There's a window in the classroom.

exercises.prompt: Fill in هَاد, هَيّ or هَدُول.
Add اَل and write how it's pronounced.
